analysis.one_liner: Requires federal investigations of serious train derailments and raises minimum railroad safety fines.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Federal Railroad Administration to thoroughly investigate every train collision or derailment that released hazardous materials or killed or injured someone badly enough to need outpatient care. It would have required a fine whenever a safety-rule violation caused those outcomes, doubled the minimum fine for safety violations from $250 to $500, made railroads file annual reports on their operations (with a waiver option if the cost outweighed the safety benefit), and funded a National Academy of Sciences study of how railroad track is designed and repaired.
analysis.who_benefits: Rail workers and people who live and work near rail lines would benefit, since serious derailments and hazardous-materials releases would automatically get a federal investigation and safety violations that cause them would carry automatic fines. Passengers, communities along tracks, and emergency responders dealing with hazmat spills would also gain from better enforcement and from the track-design study, which could lead to stronger federal track standards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail workers and communities near tracks

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Railroad Administration to thoroughly investigate every train collision or derailment involving a hazardous-materials release, a fatality, or an injury requiring at least outpatient care [S2] [S3].

Requires a civil penalty for any safety-rule violation that caused a hazardous-materials release or a fatality or injury, regardless of whether the railroad knew about the violation beforehand [S2] [S3].
Doubles the minimum penalty for violations of the Federal Railroad Safety Act from $250 to $500 [S2] [S3].

Requires annual railroad reports on operations and funds a National Academy of Sciences study of the track design and repair process, including an evaluation of federal track standards as they relate to accidents [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Railroads would bear the cost of more federal investigations, automatic fines for violations tied to derailments and injuries, doubled minimum penalties, and annual reporting paperwork. The Federal Railroad Administration would need staff and resources to investigate every qualifying accident, and Congress would need to appropriate money for the track-design study.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds reporting duties for every railroad, though the Secretary of Transportation could waive a railroad's reporting requirement if compliance costs outweighed the safety benefit, and would have to report any such waiver to Congress [S3].
It imposes automatic penalties on violations regardless of whether the violator had prior knowledge, which applies strict liability to situations a railroad might not have been able to foresee [S3].
The enforcement increase is modest: the minimum fine only doubles from $250 to $500, so the bill's practical effect depends heavily on how aggressively regulators apply it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to the public are real but narrow: it targets only a defined set of serious accidents (hazmat releases, deaths, injuries needing outpatient care) and the money at stake in fines is small by industry standards. The costs to railroads are paperwork, mandatory investigations of their own accidents, and automatic penalties in serious cases — costs that only bite when a derailment or injury has already happened. On balance it is a modest, low-cost enforcement tightening, not a major restructuring of rail safety regulation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held a vote on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. John Heinz (R-PA), joined by one Democratic cosponsor, introduced the bill on May 18, 1989 [S1] [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Railroads are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory federal investigations of serious derailments, automatic penalties for safety violations tied to hazmat releases or injuries, doubled minimum fines, and annual reporting requirements. Nothing forced the Federal Railroad Administration to change its enforcement practice either.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican lead sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, and no vote was ever taken, so its level of party-based support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed automatic civil penalties when safety-rule violations caused hazardous-materials releases or injuries, doubled minimum fines, required annual operating reports, and forced federal investigations of serious derailments — costs borne by railroads. Its failure to advance left existing enforcement practice, and railroads' exposure under it, unchanged.

industries.industry: Rail track design and repair contractors
industries.note: The bill would have funded a National Academy of Sciences study of track design, approval, and repair processes that could have led to stricter federal track standards. Rail contractors would have faced scrutiny of their design and repair practices, with no direct revenue effect from the bill itself.
